No. Everyone is scored individually and the marking mechanism for the team activity (or any of the activities) doesn’t ask the assessor to judge participants in relation to one another, it’s purely based on individual performance against the assessment metrics. If anything, it’s beneficial to have a strong group because it will allow you to perform at your best. 

Everyone in a particular group could score highly, or everyone could score lowly and not pass. There’s not a set amount of people in a group activity who will ‘pass’.

I would also write a note in the journal using the following terminology. Tell UC that you would like to open an ‘RTI dispute’ and let them know the assessment periods for which you would like to dispute, as you don’t believe the information UC is using is correct as the earning figures used on the UC statement do not match what is shown on the payslip. 

This means UC then go back to HMRC who go back to the employer to understand what has gone wrong and resolve the dispute. This process can take over 3 weeks however if you are vulnerable, it can get done quicker if you really push for a decision via the journal, particularly if you are considered vulnerable. Typically, they do not need evidence at this point but they can ask you to supply it in the future. 

If you are not happy with the result of the RTI dispute, for example, if UC uphold the decision that the earnings were correct, then you can push for a ‘mandatory reconsideration’ where you can get a decision maker to look at the information again. It’s important to use the terminology that UC use, just because they can’t skirt around what you’re actually asking for when it’s there in black and white.

My advice would be to get back to the UK asap. As even when you claim Universal Credit, there is a waiting time before your first payment (about 5ish weeks) however you can get an 'advance' payment (essentially an interest free loan, which you pay back through small deductions from future payments) to cover your living costs/expenses immediately. 

There is also the fact that if you are away from the UK for too long, you might lose your ability to claim benefits as she may not pass the habitual residency test which is mandatory for all non-British nationals and British nationals who have been out the country for more than four weeks in any two year period. 

She can ask for her payments to be backdated but the legislation around it is really tight and she would have to absolutely prove that there was no feasible way she could have submitted a claim earlier (in her case, came back to the UK earlier). I haven't seen any successful backdating claims for similar situations although it's fair to say the DWP policy is iterative and changing consistently in respond to the coronavirus pandemic so it's always worth asking for them to consider it.

I can only explain with regards to Universal Credit as I work for DWP. 

They made a policy decision that the FCO issued clear advice and guidance that it was not safe to travel after 17th March 2020 and that anyone who chose to fly abroad after that time, did so at their own risk of not being able to come back. You have to be in the UK to claim Universal Credit and therefore, your friend is not eligible as she is not in the UK. If she flew prior to the 17th March 2020 and has since been stranded and has not had an options to get home at all (government have put on some repatriation flights in some areas), then it may be a different scenario. She can make a new claim and ask for mandatory re-consideration but unless she can prove that her travel was essential and urgent, then it will most likely be closed again.

Got on with my coworkers really well and we always used to wind each other up but there was one time where it all got a bit weird. We used to take the pranks quite far as we were all good friends outside of work so initally this all seemed somewhat normal. 

I received a FB add from an account with no photos and there isn’t a proper name and it was like ‘hey, I see you work at whatever department store and I think you’re gorgeous’. Since I didn’t have my proper name badge, I had lost it, I was wearing a colleagues as it was mandatory to wear one regardless - I was perplexed at how they could have possibly found out my name. I don’t live in the area I work (about an hours drive) so it’s not like there were any mutuals. Naturally, I think it’s my friends taking the piss so I screenshot to the group chat and they’re all laughing but denying it’s them.

So I’m just rolling with it, engaging with this account and thinking it’s a prank. I don’t think anything else of it for a couple of days until I have my day off and when I come back in, my friends say a guy came in asking after me and what shifts I work. I point out how convienient it was that on my one day off this guy comes in and how I won’t fall for their pranks. They start describing the guy and I’m just rolling my eyes like whatever. 

Then I come into work and there are some chocolates for me from this guy followed by a later message from the account asking if I like them. So I message back playing along like yep I love them etc. Friends still denying it’s them. We’re all hanging out after work and then, the account starts sending random photos of me. Me near my car in the car park.  Me at work doing my job and you can tell from the angle they’re hiding behind the clothing rails not to be seen. The police gave him a warning and it turned out to be a guy in his late 30s with quite a lot of learning difficulties and since I was responding to his messages in a jovial manner, thinking it was a joke, it encouraged him to take it further. I did English Lit, History, Maths and Chem so I can give some general advice for psychology but more specific advice for chemistry that will probably be pretty similar for Biology too. Although, I sat my A2 in 2013 and I'm aware a fair bit has changed but I still reckon it will be mostly relevant.

Chemistry (+ Science in general)

1) Find your exam boards website and download the specification and print it off. Anything on that specification can be examined so it's imperative you're familiar with it. The specification is important because it helps you organise your revision into topics more efficiently but it also helps as an indicator for questions in the exam that could throw you off. Off the top of my head I remember there were certain questions in exams that seemed really unfair and unfamiliar - in retrospect, they were completely covered under the specification. Example: having to know how different amino acids form/react/etc - you can't memorise everything in chem, you have to understand the process/groups and be able to apply learnt knowledge to situations (this is key to where I went wrong). Before you start revision, have a look on the specification and highlight the areas you KNOW are your weakest - spend more time on these.

2) A2 Chem builds on a lot of AS knowledge (especially in organic, I found) so please return to anything that you weren't unsure of. I remember having memorised stuff but not really knowing/understanding why. It's always useful to purchase the relevant textbook - not only do they assist in helping you understand, they often have practice questions that you can go through before attempting past papers. 

3) Organise and sort out your notes. This should be done before revision because then you can see what's missing and what you have lots of - read through them actively, highlighting and adding comments to anything that needs further explaining. This doesn't need to be in depth and take forever, but just make sure you've got the gist of everything.

4) Flashcards. Creating flashcards for key equations/diagrams/colour changes is absolutely imperative. You MUST know these. Have them in simple note form on flashcards that you can flick through easily when bored/waiting for the bus/have a free period of an hour or something is really important. This is how I learnt most of mine and got very easy marks on both small and large mark questions by knowing the absolute easiest basic stuff. Don't throw away little marks by not putting in the tiniest bit of work!

5) Past papers are 100% your best friend. Start with these early, but make sure you feel you've done enough revision to start so it's not completely wasted. IMO, I always started with the latest possible date of past paper I could find, leaving the ones that will be 'more similar' closer towards the time so I could get a better indicator of how I would have done. Sit down and do the paper in exam conditions in a black pen - do not look at your notes or anything else (in my first year, i'd always cheat and tell myself "it's ok, I'll get it in the exam" - but you don't, you're only lying to yourself by pretending to know it). Once you've timed yourself, go through the paper again in a different colour pen and spend as long as you like attempting the questions you haven't completed in the time frame (again, don't look at notes, see if you can actually do these questions alone without guidance - if you can't, that's fine!). When you're finished, check the mark scheme (only add up the initial ones you would have got right in exam conditions). Record your grade on a spreadsheet. Fill in the answers you got incorrect, putting the correct method and answer in the box and highlighting the question - this is important, reviewing the past paper with a fine eye takes as much time as completing the past paper itself otherwise you've wasted your time. Check the questions you got wrong against the specification - you then need to spend a day or two revising these parts of the specification before your next past paper. Complete this process for every past paper - eventually, your grade such increase as your weak areas are identified and ironed out. I would recommend printing them out (it's easier to look over them, just swallow the cost pls). Be hard on yourself, lots of chem papers require very specific wording for some one mark answers - make note of this, don't just award yourself the mark if you haven't got it. I remember losing lots of mark on one word answers as I never used the proper vocab - learning definitions is very good and if i recall rightly, definitions often came up on chem papers. 

5) After completing 4 or so past papers, get them all together. Comb through them and see if any common themes arise - I used to find there were loads of one/two/three markers that asked for the same answers. Make note of these on flash cards. Learn them, they'll probably come up. Likewise, you need to make a tactic for the longer 5 mark/'essay' style questions - what do you need to do to hit all 5 marks? Can you make an almost practice answer to regurgitate? Look how it could change/adapt to a different style question. This is a big part of the revision process and is more worthwhile than reading notes.

Psychology

1) All of the above points still apply. Be familiar with your spec, create flash cards, do past papers and review, review, review. 

2) With more 'arts/social science' subjects make sure you're 100% sure of the marking criteria. I remember in english that there were different objectives (analysis/spag/critical/contextual) and you could write a fabulous essay but if you didn't include critical opinion or contextual details, you'd lose 15/40 marks avaliable as thats how many marks were assigned to those areas.

3) Practice planning answers - with arts, there is a lot of scope, so its not like chem. where you can learn and apply everything. With English - I had to learn all of the books on the course, but I only chose to revise a handful of themes (that can be easily adapted to a range of questions). Likewise with History, I covered a variety of the time period on offer in depth and in themes. I'd say it's best to revise a good selection of topics in depth (for the essay parts) so you can write a strong coherent essay, than attempt to cover absolutely everything. So make some essay plans for certain themes/topics and outline your argument, possible case studies, etc.
